subjects.displayTitle: Stories and anecdotes: learning to see again
subjects.introduction: Jesus stops beside a rotting dog and remarks on the whiteness of its teeth. An old gardener plants date palms he will never harvest and talks a caliph out of his treasury. A grieving Arab weeps over his dying dog, yet will not share his bread with it. Stories like these do not argue; they catch us in the middle of a judgment and turn the judgment around. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá told them constantly, on the road, at table, in prison and in the drawing rooms of the West, because a well-placed anecdote reaches a habit of mind that no instruction touches: the generosity that costs nothing, the piety that flees the moment the Imam hands over his horse, the courtier who praises verses he privately despises. A story may be revealed scripture, a remembered conversation or folk wisdom whose history no one can verify and whose moral no one can miss. To follow it further is to walk into humour and jokes, into the dreams and visions that so often carry its meaning, and into the recollections of the early believers, whose lives were themselves the hardest stories to hear.

questions: Which story most changed your first judgment of a person or situation? What details created that change, and how might the same habit of attention affect an ordinary encounter?

How do the accounts of shared bread, hospitality, planting trees and the grieving dog owner distinguish feeling, intention and action? Where does generosity ask for something more demanding than approval or sympathy?
What can humor reveal that a direct instruction might leave untouched? How can we recognize ourselves in these stories without using their characters to belittle other people?

How does your reading change when a passage is a revealed text, a recorded talk, a reported recollection, a dream, a parable or an epic allusion? What can be learned from a story while leaving questions about its historical foundation open?

How do the accounts of forbearance, persecution and spiritual heroism reshape the meaning of strength? What becomes clearer when personal non-retaliation is read with the stated responsibility to restrain wrongdoing and the image of lions that give life?

What do the two primary comparative readings reveal about the possibilities and limits of retelling? Which connected subject—humor, dreams and visions, the apostles, early Islamic history, poetry, or recollections of ‘Abdu’l-Baha’s life—would help you investigate a question that remains?

references.label: 1 · Luke 18:9–14 · A story that questions its reader
references.note: Luke introduces the Pharisee and the tax collector as a challenge to people who trust in their own righteousness and despise others. The contrast between their prayers ends in a reversal of expected standing before God. Read the Gospel passage beside the retelling near the beginning of this guide. How does the opening frame change the way we hear the story? Compare other anecdotes in which the confident judge becomes the person whose judgment needs examination. A reading that merely assigns someone else the role of the Pharisee may evade the question the parable asks of its reader.

references.label: 2 · SN 35.88, Punna Sutta · Meeting hostility without hatred
references.note: In this Buddhist discourse, Punna prepares to teach in Sunaparanta. The Buddha questions him about possible insults and increasingly severe violence; his replies show how he intends to maintain self-control. Compare this exchange with the compilation’s reported story of the Buddha questioning his disciples. The canonical discourse concerns Punna individually and places the encounter within instruction about suffering and release; the retelling uses a different religious vocabulary. The translator’s note distinguishes accepting the possibility of death from seeking it. What can the comparison illuminate about freedom from hatred, and what differences should remain visible?
